Published by Putangi Publications, this substantial volume compiles the pioneering field logs, letters, and bird observations of Richard Henry—Aotearoa New Zealand's legendary pioneer conservationist and caretaker of Resolution Island in Fiordland. 

Henry was the first person in the world to attempt island sanctuary translocations to save endangered flightless species like the kākāpō and kiwi from introduced predators (stoats and ferrets). This rich collection offers detailed historical accounts of early wildlife management, Fiordland geography, and original natural history observations across Te Anau, Dusky Sound, and Kāpiti Island.

listings.title: Moriori A People Rediscovered Michael King NZ History & Rekohu Culture REVISED
listings.body:
Moriori A People Rediscovered

Moriori: A People Rediscovered by Michael King is a landmark historical work that restored the Moriori people of the Chatham Islands to their rightful place in New Zealand and world history. In this award-winning account, King decisively strips away long-standing myths and vilification, identifying clearly who the Moriori were and where they originated. The narrative explores the unique adaptation of Moriori culture to the harsh environment of Rekohu (the Chatham Islands) and reveals that they were not a distinct race, nor are they extinct. This book is a fascinating exercise in historical, archaeological, and literary detective work that addresses issues of identity and the resilience of a people whose mana remains intact despite a history of invasion and suffering.

Contents include:
* The Origins of Moriori
* Life on Rekohu
* The Invasion of 1835
* The Enslavement
* European Contact and the Law
* The Native Land Court
* The Struggle for Survival
* The Modern Resurgence
* Moriori Vocabulary 
* Bibliography
* Index

This extensive study provides a clear and honest history of the Chatham Islands, documented through waiata, genealogy, and historical stories. It is illustrated with many rare historical photographs and maps that provide a visual record of the Moriori experience.


Keywords: Moriori Michael King Chatham Islands Rekohu NZ History New Zealand Indigenous Rekohu Maori Invasion Polynesian Genealogy Moriori Culture Pacific History Chatham Island Photos Ethnography

This regional publication provides an account of the domestic, agricultural, and civic evolution of the Central Moutere district. The book delivers structured chronological documentation concerning the arrival, land acquisition, and initial clearing operations executed by early German and European immigrant populations who settled the area from 1843 onward. It covers the structural transition from subsistence farming to commercial orchards, viticulture, hops cultivation, and pastoral agriculture. Comprehensive data sets trace the administrative decisions of early road boards, school committees, and local governing councils. Specific reference material incorporates complete reproductions of early cadastral maps showing original section allotments, land grant titles, and changing property boundaries over successive generations. The book features extensive appendices containing systematic family registers, complete early school enrollment rolls, and chronological lists of local public officials. It incorporates numerous historical photographs alongside detailed architectural drawings of early homesteads, community halls, and church buildings. The research relies on local parish records, provincial council gazettes, family diaries, and land registry records to assemble an absolute timeline of district development.

Compiled with a focus on archival records, the volume covers early Polynesian exploration, subsequent maritime arrivals, and regional settlement patterns.

listings.body:
EXPLORING NEW ZEALAND'S GHOST RAILWAYS

Grantham House Publishing, Wellington, 1998. Softback. 127 pages


Railway enthusiasts, casual walkers, dedicated trampers, historians, those who can recall the heyday of New Zealand railways- all will be delighted by this lively, superbly researched guide to New Zealand's ghost railways

Authors David Leitch and Brian Scott provide a brief but thorough history of each ghost line's construction and use, before giving detailed, easily followed guides to exploring what remains- from the comfort of a car and on foot. The rail system was once the lifeblood of New Zealand, connecting the people and produce of remote settlements and rural areas with ports, industries, towns and cities. 

Largely gone now are the many small, often busy, branch and main lines that criss-crossed the landscape, and the little stations that became the centres of their communities, but the remains of these lines have left a fascinating legacy. As this attractively illustrated book shows, discovering ghost railways is a journey into an intriguing aspect of New Zealand's past when the railway ruled the land. 

 First published in 1995, this is the revised edition.

Ask That Mountain: The Story of Parihaka - Dick Scott

This volume documents the history of the Parihaka settlement at the foot of Mount Taranaki, tracing the nineteenth-century Māori passive resistance movement and subsequent state interventions. 

The book outlines regional conflicts and military campaigns that divided the territory, examining the social environment under leaders Te Whiti o Rongomai and Tohu Kākahi. Entries detail the defensive measures used by the community, including the actions of Māori ploughmen and fencers along regional roads. The chapters compile historical documentation on the expansion of land confiscations, the challenge of the ploughmen, the battle of the fences, and the events leading up to the structural breakdown of the village.

It records the mobilization of the Parihaka expeditionary force on 5 November 1881, tracking the movements of the 2,000 soldiers who entered the settlement. It details the subsequent military occupation, the arrest and exile of community leaders, and the introduction of pass laws and forced pilgrimages. Archival photographic plates document contemporary figures, including Mete Kīngi Paetahi in Christchurch, children within the settlement, and armed constabulary road-builders clad in altered attire for regional movement alongside Captain Henry Morrison and Major Foster Goring. The appendices compile specific data including historical portraits of Te Whiti, records of the Taranaki drink trade, and the text of Hiroki's final letter.

THE CHOPPER BOYS

The Chopper Boys by Rex Forrester is a thrilling account of New Zealand’s pioneering helicopter hunting era. This book captures the raw energy, danger, and ingenuity of the men who transformed deer recovery into a high-flying industry. Forrester, a legendary outdoorsman and storyteller, chronicles the rise of commercial venison recovery and the role helicopters played in reshaping the landscape of hunting in Aotearoa.

Set in the rugged backcountry of the 1960s and 70s, the book follows the evolution of deer hunting from ground-based stalking to aerial operations. It explores the development of techniques for spotting, shooting, and retrieving deer carcasses using helicopters, and the emergence of a new breed of hunter—part cowboy, part pilot, all adrenaline. The narrative is packed with real-life stories of daring chopper maneuvers, close calls, and the camaraderie among hunters and crew.

He introduces readers to the “meat hawks,” the “cowboys of the deer squadrons,” and the “jet-age professionals” who helped build a multimillion-dollar industry from the skies

listings.title: When The World Was Young - Eliza Rockel A Pioneer Of Turakina
listings.body:
from the web ...

Mrs. Eliza Rockel. of Wanganui, one of the oldest living New Zealand-born women, if not the oldest, celebrated her ninety-sixth birthday on Monday. Mrs. Rockel's memory is excellent, and she has given much interesting and useful information to local historians. 

Mrs. Rockel's parents were Mr. and Mrs. T. V. McKenzie, who were married in Wellington when Mrs. McKenzie was 16. Mrs. Rockel was one of the five children born in Wellington before 1846. In 1850 the family set out for their land at Turakina. "A horse and cart were hired, but the driver refused to ford the Manawatu River, so the family walked the rest of the way, escorted by Napier Tara toa. Mrs. McKenzie rode on a horse lent by Dr. Best. To cross the Rangitikei River, fishermen's panniers were put on each side of the horse, and in these the children were placed.

Living in clay and slab whares, breaking in the land, sledging supplies, butter, eggs, and honey, down the coast to the little schooners, all this is part of Mrs. Rockel's memories. The old "Poynzfield" garden (the McKenzie place) was unrivalled on the coast; today it is part of Flock House station From there Mrs. Rockel was married. She had a family of eight boys and four girls, and today her descendants number nearly 300

Written by Thomas W Downes (1868–1938), this collection of stories captures the historical & cultural essence of the Whanganui River region. Downes, a respected historian & river works supervisor, dedicated much of his life to documenting the lives, landscapes & legends surrounding the river. 

Originally prepared for publication in 1938, the manuscript was not published until 1995 by The Friends of the Whanganui River.

This 149-page volume includes a range of narratives that reflect the unique character of the river & its people. Downes’ deep connection to the region is evident throughout, offering insights into Māori traditions, early European settlement, river navigation & local folklore. His firsthand experience as a ranger & supervisor for the Wanganui River Trust lends authenticity to the accounts.

The book is illustrated & includes a map, enhancing the reader’s understanding of the geographical context. It serves as both a historical record & a tribute to the enduring significance of the Whanganui River in New Zealand’s heritage. The stories are accessible & informative, making it suitable for readers interested in regional history, Māori culture, or river ecology.

This edition was published in 1995 It was issued by The Friends of the Whanganui River, a group committed to preserving the river’s legacy. The publication reflects a collaborative effort to honour Downes’ work & ensure its availability to future generations.

listings.title: Wanganui in 1911  A Coronation Souvenir Of Wanganui Buisnesses
listings.body:
Wanganui in 1911  A Coronation Souvenir

This 148-page facsimile reproduction was published by the Whanganui Regional Heritage Trust in 2012.

In 1911 Wanganui was marketing itself as being “Pretty, Prosperous and Progressive”.  The combined population of the four boroughs and town councils that made up “Greater Wanganui” was just under 15,000, more than both Palmerston North and New Plymouth at the time.  Local citizens considered Wanganui was destined to become a large city and the Borough Council was developing essential infrastructure such as the port, tram system, gas and water supplies to cope with the needs of a growing population.

The coronation of King George V and Queen Mary on 22 June 1911 was an occasion for celebration throughout the British Empire.  In New Zealand, the coronation was marked by an industrial exhibition in Wellington and the government provided grants to encourage local authorities to erect public facilities to commemorate the occasion.  As a result, memorial halls, libraries, gates and band rotundas were built throughout the country. In Wanganui, the Borough Council took advantage of the funds on offer to build a Coronation Band Rotunda on a prominent site at its newest public park, Virginia Lake, and published a pictorial Coronation Souvenir to promote the growing town.

Covers Many small and large Buisnesses in the City with write-ups and many photographs of early shopfronts

This volume presents the biographical notes and family reminiscences of Leonard Owen Howard Tripp, detailing the nineteenth-century pioneer history of his family in Christchurch and the South Canterbury region. 

The text was compiled and edited by Barbara Harper of Woodbury, incorporating dictated notes from Tripp alongside an earlier account titled "My Early Days" written by his mother, Mrs. Charles Tripp (Ellen Harper). Around the north-east of the Kaippara harbour author Dick Scott encountered the remarkable histories of seven families who had been in close contact with the Ngati Whatua during the early days of European settlement. 

In Seven Lives On Salt River he seeks out to find out who these people were, what beliefs they brought with them from Europe and how they adapted to a new land. 

Each family, in some way, left it's mark, like the Blackwells who were largely responsible for the botanical classic, Laing and Blackwells Plants of New Zealand. W Heathcote Jackman, the first successful grower of classic grapes - a success that owed something to his use of ground Maori bones for fertiliser.... 

Winner of the 1988 NZ Book Award 

But beyond the achievements and legacies of the families, it is the details of how they interacted with their new land and its Maori inhabitants that gives this book its fascination. It features more than 100 previously unpublished photos.

listings.title: The Trekka Dynasty New Zealand's Only Designed + Built Car
listings.body:
The Trekka Dynasty New Zealand's Only Built Car 

The Trekka was launched on 2 December 1966 as an agricultural vehicle although it eventually became popular with both rural buyers and urban tradesmen. The first Trekkas were sold in New Zealand in 1967, by which time Motor Lines had become Motor Holdings. The first model sold was the "2-10", which cost less than a Morris 1100 at just £899.

 The 2-10s were all painted green with canvas tops and were offered with a tow bar as the only option.

Initially, the Trekka was produced at a rate of six vehicles a day with hand-formed steel panels. Production output increased after the panel forming was contracted out to H J Ryans, an Auckland manufacturer of lawn mowers. 708 Trekkas were sold in its first year of production and by January 1968 the 1,000th had been manufactured. When production ceased in 1973, some 2,500 had been built.

Buyer demand for a more weather-proof top was answered by a white fibreglass canopy, whose manufacture was outsourced to another Auckland company. These later models were also fitted with improved seats.

listings.title: Teak And Tide The Ebbs and Eddies Of The Edwin Fox   272 pages VG condition
listings.body:
The book took 4 years to write...

The tale of the Edwin Fox was a rich human interest story, he said. It's had such a versatile career. There's just a lot of colour and drama in the story that I was able to pick up on.

Marlborough mayor Alistair Sowman formally launched the book on 9 December 2014.

Mr Sowman said the Edwin Fox was a real treasure for Marlborough. Not only did it bring early European settlers to the province, but it played a key role in building New Zealand's early trade in refrigerated meat. This is a timely reminder of the history we have in Picton and Marlborough as a whole. In addition when we first heard about the book, we realised that it's not just local or national - there's international interest in this subject.

The Edwin Fox was built in 1853 in Sulkeali on the Hooghly River in India and sold to Duncan Dunbar II in 1854. It is the world's ninth oldest wooden troop ship and was used to carry soldiers to the Crimea War (1853-1856), convicts to Australia and bring immigrants from Britain to New Zealand. In the 1880s steam arrived and Edwin Fox was fitted out as a floating freezer hulk and used in several New Zealand ports.

In 1897, it was towed to Picton and used as a freezer ship and then as a coal hulk. The ship was virtually derelict when the Edwin Fox Society took it on as a project. The New Zealand Historic Places Trust placed a category-one listing on the ship.

Waitaki Dammed - The Building Of The Waitaki Dam 1927 - 

Work began on the Waitaki Dam, the first large state hydroelectric scheme in the South Island since Lake Coleridge, in mid-1928 at a site 7 km from the Kurow railhead. It was the last major dam built by pick, shovel and wheelbarrow, tools anachronistically retained because politicians wanted to reduce the unemployment rate. At its peak 1200 men laboured in often dangerous and freezing conditions; 350 houses and 700 huts sheltered them from the extremes of North Otago winters, but work conditions and high accident rates made Waitaki a bleak site.

listings.title: The History of Old New Zealand Houses 1800-1940 by Jeremy Salmond
listings.body:
The History of Old New Zealand Houses 1800-1940 by Jeremy Salmond 

Softcovered VG condition

Old New Zealand Houses 1800 - 1940 by Jeremy Salmond

They appear everywhere in the New Zealand landscape, a wonderfully distinctive collection of older houses in all shapes and sizes, ranked along city or small-town streets or dotted across farming hillsides and by country roads.

This book is both a history and a celebration of New Zealand's magnificent old houses, a clear and approachable account of how these houses were made and inhabited.

Above all it is an account of the methods used in their construction - from traditional Maori dwellings and the earliest European houses of cob and adobe, to the rise of the 'kitset' villa building industry in the later half of the nineteenth century.

 It chronicles the impact of the Californian and Spanish bungalows, the 'arts and crafts' cottages, and the quirky Modernes built in New Zealand before World War II. Significantly, this account ends with the introduction of the state house.

Jeremy Salmond's book is sumptuously illustrated with old and new photographs and exact technical drawings.

 Extracts from contemporary letters, diaries and trade literature evoke the qualities admired in each major house style.

This genealogical history book documents the ancestral lineage, migration, and centennial tracking of William and Sarah Spurdle (née Sibley). The text outlines the family origins within Seaborough, a border parish in Somerset, England, tracing regional church and vestry records on vellum dating back to the 15th century. Included within the documentation are observations of parish register gaps circa 1740 during the rise of the Methodist movement under the Wesleys and Whitfield, alongside oval portrait reproductions of the original pioneer subjects, William and Sarah Spurdle.

listings.body:
Bush Burn To Butter by Eric Warr.

by Eric Warr

An illustrated history of the New Zealand dairy industry from its first beginnings in New Zealand to the modern day.

New Zealand is recognised as having one of the most efficient dairy industries in the world and the modern dairy industry, based on approximately two million dairy cows in 16,000 herds is a major export industry and of critical importance to New Zealand's future.

One of his most passionate interests was the history and development of the New Zealand dairy industry. He spent many years courageously battling ill health, researching the subject and gathering photographic material for the book he intended to write. From Bush-Burn to Butter is the result of his years of research and labour. His death in early 1988 meant that Eric could not be involved in the latter stages of the book and some information has unfortunately been lost to us, most notably his bibliography. The resultant work is, however, a fitting memorial to a man who worked so hard to uncover the industrial developments and social history of an industry which today is still one of New Zealand's most important income earners.

listings.body:
The History of Old New Zealand Houses 1800-1940 by Jeremy Salmond 

Hardback 1980 first edition 

Old New Zealand Houses 1800 - 1940 by Jeremy Salmond

They appear everywhere in the New Zealand landscape, a wonderfully distinctive collection of older houses in all shapes and sizes, ranked along city or small-town streets or dotted across farming hillsides and by country roads.

This book is both a history and a celebration of New Zealand's magnificent old houses, a clear and approachable account of how these houses were made and inhabited.

Above all it is an account of the methods used in their construction - from traditional Maori dwellings and the earliest European houses of cob and adobe, to the rise of the 'kitset' villa building industry in the later half of the nineteenth century.

 It chronicles the impact of the Californian and Spanish bungalows, the 'arts and crafts' cottages, and the quirky Modernes built in New Zealand before World War II. Significantly, this account ends with the introduction of the state house.

Jeremy Salmond's book is sumptuously illustrated with old and new photographs and exact technical drawings.

 Extracts from contemporary letters, diaries and trade literature evoke the qualities admired in each major house style.

My Own Story, An Episode in the Life of a New Zealand Settler of 50 years back. - Brett Printing and Publishing Company

Retrospective

This book provides a personal autobiographical account of a female pioneer immigrant who departed England in 1848 to settle in early Auckland. The text documents her early life on the banks of the Thames, her marriage, and the financial circumstances involving a legal trustee that led her husband to abandon his career at the English Bar to emigrate.

The records detail the subsequent four-month maritime passage to the South Pacific aboard a vessel carrying sixty passengers. It provides historical observations of Auckland as it appeared upon their arrival, describing a primitive town populated by approximately 4,000 residents. The early infrastructure is documented, noting the absence of a wharf, the use of small lighters for discharging ships, a wooden gangway, and the location of the Victoria Hotel.

This historical book provides a first-hand account of early colonial life and inter-cultural relations in the Hokianga district during the nineteenth century. The book documents the observations of an early European settler who integrated into a northern tribe, detailing traditional social structures, customary protocols, and economic trade systems prior to the establishment of formal colonial government. It outlines the specific dynamics of early cross-cultural interactions along the coast.

The historical coverage records key political and military events in the northern region, including the 1840 interactions with Governor Hobson surrounding the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi. Factual accounts document participation within northern war campaigns against Hone Heke, detailing tribal alliances, military movements, and tactical developments. Additional biographical and institutional data covers the author's later civic duties as a judge within the Native Land Court, tracking legal frameworks, property disputes, and the accelerating transition toward European legal administrative dominance.

listings.title: Cascade on the Run  A Season With The Whitebaiters of South Westland
listings.body:
Cascade on the Run Whitebaiters of South Westland
by Neville Peat 

 Black and white photos, Maps, 126 pages including two appendices, bibliography, index, b/w photos throughout, double spread photographic title pages, maps, fish sketch. 

Hard Cover. First edition.

some wear to the cover - internally VG 

The setting is an isolated camp at the mouth of the Cascade River in South Westland. Each spring a select small group of families and friends, who for almost 30 years have fished on the Lower Cascade, fly in to this unique settlement from all parts of the South Island.

These Cascaders are a special kind of whitebaiter – a close knit community of men and women who have pioneered their own style of fishing, independent f motor vehicles and bodily removed NZ society. 

Neville Peat gives an absorbing account of these whitebaiters’ lives ‘on the run’: the race to prepare boats, stands and nets before opening day; the rewards and disappointments of the ‘daily dance’ on the catwalks lining the big river; the comforts and camaraderie back at the cottages. He peppers his story with yarns about boating and hunting adventures. Later, when dealing with the processing, transport and marketing of whitebait in the air age, he recounts some of the hair-raising exploits of pilots who have flown the Cascade shuttle since 1954.

 discovery, exploration and settlement attempts in the area, then rounds off his survey by recording the enterprise and ingenuity of the Buchanan brothers who developed the Cascade fishery in the 1940s.

listings.title: Memories of World War II Stewart Frame DFC
listings.body:
Memories of World War II Stewart Frame


In Quietness And Confidence


Memories of World War II
Author	Stewart Frame
Edition	illustrated

Publisher	Stewart Frame, 2013 92 pages with photos 

Stewart served in the campaign as a pilot with the Royal Air Force flying Mark 8 Wellington aircraft.  

After training with the Royal New Zealand Air Force, he was posted overseas and joined up with the RAF.  He served with distinction as a pilot and was later awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross during operations in Malta. 

He has often told the story about having to ditch in the sea during the war as a result of engine failure.  Stewart and his squadron were trained for coastal command and search missions and to locate enemy shipping, including U boats.  With an engine failure an hour out from Sicily, the crew sent out a mayday call, and Stewart managed to put the Wellington down on a good sea.  

The tail touched the water and then the aircraft nose-dived and all went quiet.  “I thought at first, this is heaven.  My co-pilot and I got up out of the aircraft and stepped onto a life raft without even getting wet”.  They were fortunately rescued by an allied ship and within a few days were back on active service.  

Excellent condition

This local history publication contains papers and documentation regarding the Whanganui district and its surrounding regions. The book opens with studies on regional church architecture, detailing structural designs and early parishes, followed by historical overviews marking 150 years of settlement in the area. Specific papers focus on the history of St George Lowther, an account of an incident on the Wanganui River, and an analysis of water problems originating from Virginia Lake. Cultural and economic histories are addressed through a profile on the Wanganui River Annual, an investigation into Ayrshire House, and genealogical records concerning the Brechin family and Tom Boswall Williams. Photographic plates and sketches depict St Oswald's Church at Westmere, St Martin's at Greatford, St George's at Patea, All Saints at Wanganui East, All Saints at Palmerston North, alongside commercial premises on Rutland Street and portraits of early business founders.

listings.title: Historical Record Vol 21 No 1 May 1990 Journal Whanganui Historical Society Inc
listings.body:
This twenty-first anniversary issue contains a compiled selection of papers documenting the social, industrial, and infrastructural history of the Whanganui district. The book opens with an examination of Koriniti Pa, followed by historical overviews of the purchase of Wanganui and regional place names. Early agricultural development is covered via an account of Wanganui River farms, alongside coastal history detailing Scott's Ferry and the establishment of local dame schools. Regional transport networks are documented through specialized papers on early railways and tramways, complemented by an overview of the Port of Wanganui operations. Biographical profiles detail the lives of local figures Granny Dalton and John Cameron, supplemented by historical recipes and a study on the development of Durie Hill. Photographic plates and archival illustrations include a 1880 Burton Brothers image of Koriniti Pa, a horse bus to Aramoho, a Takapuna tram, a portrait of Rangi Pokiha, portraits of Granny Dalton, the remnants of Tram No 1, the Port of Wanganui in 1887, the Durie Hill time ball, and Miss Ramsay's Dame School.

listings.title: Vol 23 Number 1 Wanganui Historical Record  May 1992
listings.body:
This local history journal compiles research papers and historical accounts concerning maritime, industrial, and social activities in the Whanganui district. The book features a comprehensive overview of regional commerce titled Trading in Wanganui through the years, followed by a study on timber rafting on the Whanganui river. Maritime history is documented through a detailed reconstruction of the wreck of the Cyrena at Wanganui in 1925 and an account of childhood memories at the port of Castlecliff. Religious and social history is covered via a record of the Sisters of Compassion centennial pilgrimage. Photographic plates and illustrations include the inauguration of the tug and barge service in August 1991, a timber raft ready to be launched at Taumarunui, departure from Taumarunui, and the raft just before arrival at Wanganui. Maritime disaster plates depict the Cyrena berthing at Wellington, the vessel after breaking in two, the stern section against the north mole, the demolition process, and the remaining engines, alongside images of the Port Bowen aground at Castlecliff and scenes from the Sisters of Compassion pilgrimage.

listings.title: Historical Record Vol 20 No 2 Nov 1989 Journal Whanganui Historical Society Inc
listings.body:
This regional history journal compiles research papers focusing on the military, agricultural, industrial, and cultural developments within the Whanganui district. The book opens with an analysis of military operations titled The Tussock Campaign of 1869, followed by an agricultural overview documenting regional horticulture with specific focus on Parnells. Biographical research details the life and estate of Charles Rowe of Marangai. Industrial history is examined via a dedicated study of regional flaxmilling activities spanning 1870 to 1874. Maori history and river ethnography are documented in the paper Te Awa Nui A Rua, followed by a record of the society winter programme from 1989. Visual plates and photographic illustrations by Judith Crawley complement the papers, featuring a scenic view of the Wanganui River on the cover, a view of Fraserfield Private Cemetery, a depiction of Scott's Ferry Landing, and architectural views of the exterior and interior of Wheriko Church at Parawanui, alongside botanical studies of a Te Kouka tree, a Karaka tree, a Tasmanian Gum, and a Hoop Pine.

listings.title: Whanganui Historical Record Journal Vol 12 No 1 May 1981 Mangamahu Napier
listings.body:
Historical Record Vol. 12 No. 1 May 1981 - Whanganui Historical Society Inc.

This regional publication contains documented local history compiled by the society. The contents comprise research papers, biographical logs, and regional archival transcriptions relating to colonial governance, educational institutions, exploration, and provincial development within the wider district and surrounding regions.

Contents:
* Early Wanganui Government Officials - R.M. Startup, Pages 1-3
* Restoration of Rev. Taylor's Grave - Page 3
* Punishment by Exile - A.L. Kirk, Pages 4-8
* 140th Anniversary of Wanganui - Page 8
* Prospecting up the Wanganui River 1884 - Pages 9-12
* Book Review A Farm on the Wanganui River - E. Allen, Page 12
* Te Aute College - Pages 13-16
* Cathedral Church of St. John the Evangelist Napier - Page 16
* Visit to Hawkes Bay - Pages 17-18
* Garden Party - Page 18
* Mangamahu 1981 - Page 19
* Early History - Page 19
* Study tour of Northland, Bay of Plenty & East Coast - Page 20

The primary research papers in this volume examine the identities and roles of early municipal and government officials in the district, alongside legal histories tracking judicial practices such as penal exile. Specific investigative sections cover mineral prospecting expeditions along the upper river reaches during 1884 and the legacy of Te Aute College. Ecclesiastical updates note the conservation of the Reverend Taylor sepulcher and the architectural heritage of the Cathedral Church of St. John the Evangelist in Napier. Travel diaries document domestic study tours through Hawkes Bay, Northland, the Bay of Plenty, and the East Coast.

listings.title: Historical Record Vol 25 No 2 November 1994 Journal Whanganui Historical Society
listings.body:
This regional history publication contains research papers and archival documentation concerning the early religious, civic, and geographical exploration of the Whanganui district. The book opens with a major biographical study titled William Woon - Printer and Missionary, tracking early printing operations and Wesleyan Methodist mission work. Transcribed letters to the editor from 1890 record early civic perspectives, followed by an administrative report details a donation to the Wanganui Library from 1889. Land exploration and route surveying are examined in the paper The Track that Field made, which details the pathfinding activities of Henry Claylands Field. Architectural and funerary history is documented through the study An Unusual Memorial, which details a mausoleum near Mataroa, followed by an investigation into mining history titled Kaimanawa Gold. The cover features an illustration of the twin headstones of William and Jane Woon in the Heads Road cemetery, and internal illustrations detail the grave of Rev William Woon, a portrait of Henry Claylands Field, and views of the Mataroa mausoleum structure.

listings.body:
The Fatal Impact: The Invasion of the South Pacific 1767-1840 - Alan Moorehead

Contents:

This book examines European penetration into the South Pacific between 1767 and 1840, examining early contacts made during major maritime expeditions. Initial focus centres on Tahiti during initial encounters, tracking cultural changes following European arrival.

Coverage shifts to eastern Australia, detailing early landings at Botany Bay, subsequent settlement efforts, land expansion, and cultural encounters with Indigenous populations alongside ecological transformation.

The concluding sections focus on sub-Antarctic and Antarctic regions, documenting voyage routes of the HMS Resolution, early seal hunting, whaling operations, and early marine exploitation.
